The presentation moves to the “Application of Lung Ultrasound” title slide, followed by a “No Disclosures” slide and screenshots of the MetroHealth Emergency Ultrasound YouTube channel. The attributed narration introduces today’s topic, notes the disclosure statement, and points viewers to prior lectures and short teaching videos. The presentation finishes its brief channel promotion, then transitions from the MetroHealth Emergency Ultrasound YouTube page to a “Review” interstitial and a lung-ultrasound image. The attributed narration encourages viewers to subscribe and share videos, then begins a review of prior material, starting with the question of whether lung sliding is present. The presentation shows several lung-ultrasound stills focused on the pleural line beneath the ribs, then transitions to a black “A B C D E” slide. The attributed narration identifies the pleural line and describes assessing its movement with breathing as lung sliding. The sampled frames introduce an A–E mnemonic in centered and vertical layouts, then show labels for A-lines, B-lines, consolidations, and effusions while D is crossed out. A separate grayscale lung ultrasound image appears at the end. The attributed narration introduces the four findings and explains the mnemonic. The minute shows a rectangular lung ultrasound view with horizontal echoes beneath the pleural line, then switches by 345 seconds to a sector-shaped grayscale ultrasound view labeled with a “Cardiac” preset. The attributed narration discusses reverberation from the pleural line, A-lines and the introduction of B-lines. The minute begins with a sector-shaped grayscale scan labeled with a “Cardiac” preset, switches by 375 seconds to a “FAST EXAM” scan with bright vertical echoes, and ends on a different ultrasound display. The attributed narration discusses B-lines and consolidation, including changes in pleural appearance. The presentation displays several ultrasound views of the pleural and upper-abdominal region, then introduces a research article titled “International evidence-based recommendations for point-of-care lung ultrasound.” The attributed narration reviews subpleural consolidation and pleural effusion, describing fluid separating the lung from the diaphragm or chest wall. The presentation holds on the cover page of “International evidence-based recommendations for point-of-care lung ultrasound.” The attributed narration compares the 2012 international evidence-based guidelines with a 2022 revision, noting that the newer guidelines build on foundational material while standardizing terminology and machine settings and encouraging more nuanced research. The presentation remains on the cover of the international evidence-based lung-ultrasound recommendations. The attributed narration outlines three topics for the talk: lung sliding, A-versus-B profiles, and consolidation, and says these findings will be considered together with clinical information. The presentation continues to show the cover of the international evidence-based lung-ultrasound recommendations. In the attributed narration, the speaker contrasts lung ultrasound, which interprets artifacts produced by the lung, with exams that directly show anatomy and pathology, then explains that lung-ultrasound profiles can overlap across conditions and do not map one-to-one to diagnoses such as pneumonia. The recommendation cover page remains on screen throughout. In the attributed narration, the speaker says clinicians combine lung-ultrasound findings with the patient’s clinical presentation, use overlapping profiles to weigh possibilities such as pneumonia, atelectasis, contusion, or fibrosis, and frames bedside ultrasound as collecting information at the bedside to support decisions. The recommendations cover remains through the first three Locals. The final frame of [750,760) introduces an “Evaluation for Pneumothorax” title slide; [760,780) shows a list of four sonographic findings: absent lung sliding, lung point, absent B-lines, and absent lung pulse. The attributed narration transitions to pneumothorax evaluation. The first three Local windows show the black slide listing four pneumothorax findings. [810,820) shows that slide before a white decision flowchart at 819 seconds; [820,840) shows paired grayscale lung ultrasound images, after a flowchart frame at 821 seconds. The attributed narration discusses lung sliding, its limited specificity when absent alone, and use of other findings such as lung point in a decision process. The visuals alternate between a pneumothorax decision flowchart, grayscale lung-ultrasound images, the four-findings list, and paired ultrasound images. In the attributed narration, the speaker describes the lung point as an edge where movement is seen on one side and absent on the other, then begins discussing B-lines as reverberation artifacts between pleural layers. Paired grayscale lung-ultrasound images dominate the visuals; a pneumothorax decision flowchart briefly reappears before the final ultrasound image. In the attributed narration, the speaker explains how B-line artifacts relate to pleural opposition and says their presence can help rule against pneumothorax, then introduces lung pulse as the final finding. A single grayscale lung-ultrasound view remains on screen throughout this block. In the attributed narration, the speaker describes lung pulse as faint rhythmic movement transmitted from the beating heart, says it is absent with pneumothorax, and recaps the absent signs used in the pneumothorax decision tree. The minute shows an “Evaluation of Interstitial Syndrome” title with intermittent black frames, then a “Definition of B Lines” slide from 1069 seconds. The definition slide lists discrete laser-like projections from the pleural line, reaching the bottom without fading and moving with lung sliding. The attributed narration introduces A-versus-B profiles and begins defining B-lines. The “Definition of B Lines” slide appears intermittently with black frames through the first four Locals and at the start of [1120,1130). By 1129 seconds, a “What Is a Positive Region?” slide defines a positive region as three or more B-lines in a longitudinal plane between ribs. The attributed narration discusses normal versus pathological B-line findings. The positive-region slide defines three or more B-lines between ribs in a longitudinal plane and remains through 1175 seconds. By 1179 seconds the presentation changes to a “Pathologies Associated with B Lines” list, which continues through the end of the minute. The attributed narration describes mapping positive regions and notes B-lines can occur with multiple conditions. The same black slide listing conditions associated with B-lines remains visible throughout. In the attributed narration, the speaker discusses overlap between COVID pneumonia and other interstitial pneumonia patterns, describes B-lines as a potentially helpful but nonspecific finding, and begins mentioning pulmonary fibrosis. The B-lines-associated conditions list remains through most of the block, then transitions to a “Questions to Ask” slide listing clinical scenario, unilateral versus bilateral distribution, homogeneous versus patchy pattern, and location. In the attributed narration, the speaker notes B-lines can occur across many conditions and emphasizes interpreting them in the patient’s clinical context, contrasting cough and fever with trauma. The “Questions to Ask” slide remains on screen throughout, listing clinical scenario, laterality, homogeneous versus patchy distribution, and location. In the attributed narration, the speaker explains that these questions help distinguish among possible causes of B-lines, contrasting diffuse bilateral patterns with focal or patchy findings and discussing anterior/posterior and apical/basal location. A static teaching graphic shows a torso marked with lung-zone divisions alongside annotated anterior and posterior body diagrams with numbered zones. The first Local briefly begins on the preceding “Questions to Ask” slide. In the attributed narration, the speaker introduces lung-zone mapping, describes anterior/lateral and posterior zones, and transitions toward clinical scenarios for interpreting B-profiles.

global_summary_target: The presentation opens with a MetroHealth “Ultrasound Grand Rounds” title card and a speaker inset. The attributed narration welcomes viewers, introduces the final installment of a short lung-ultrasound series, and frames the talk around applying ultrasound findings to patient decisions; it also points viewers to earlier episodes on the MetroHealth emergency-ultrasound YouTube channel. The presentation moves to the “Application of Lung Ultrasound” title slide, followed by a “No Disclosures” slide and screenshots of the MetroHealth Emergency Ultrasound YouTube channel. The attributed narration introduces today’s topic, notes the disclosure statement, and points viewers to prior lectures and short teaching videos. The presentation finishes its brief channel promotion, then transitions from the MetroHealth Emergency Ultrasound YouTube page to a “Review” interstitial and a lung-ultrasound image. The attributed narration encourages viewers to subscribe and share videos, then begins a review of prior material, starting with the question of whether lung sliding is present. The presentation shows several lung-ultrasound stills focused on the pleural line beneath the ribs, then transitions to a black “A B C D E” slide. The attributed narration identifies the pleural line and describes assessing its movement with breathing as lung sliding. The sampled frames introduce an A–E mnemonic in centered and vertical layouts, then show labels for A-lines, B-lines, consolidations, and effusions while D is crossed out. A separate grayscale lung ultrasound image appears at the end. The attributed narration introduces the four findings and explains the mnemonic. The minute shows a rectangular lung ultrasound view with horizontal echoes beneath the pleural line, then switches by 345 seconds to a sector-shaped grayscale ultrasound view labeled with a “Cardiac” preset. The attributed narration discusses reverberation from the pleural line, A-lines and the introduction of B-lines. The minute begins with a sector-shaped grayscale scan labeled with a “Cardiac” preset, switches by 375 seconds to a “FAST EXAM” scan with bright vertical echoes, and ends on a different ultrasound display. The attributed narration discusses B-lines and consolidation, including changes in pleural appearance. The presentation displays several ultrasound views of the pleural and upper-abdominal region, then introduces a research article titled “International evidence-based recommendations for point-of-care lung ultrasound.” The attributed narration reviews subpleural consolidation and pleural effusion, describing fluid separating the lung from the diaphragm or chest wall. The presentation holds on the cover page of “International evidence-based recommendations for point-of-care lung ultrasound.” The attributed narration compares the 2012 international evidence-based guidelines with a 2022 revision, noting that the newer guidelines build on foundational material while standardizing terminology and machine settings and encouraging more nuanced research. The presentation remains on the cover of the international evidence-based lung-ultrasound recommendations. The attributed narration outlines three topics for the talk: lung sliding, A-versus-B profiles, and consolidation, and says these findings will be considered together with clinical information. The presentation continues to show the cover of the international evidence-based lung-ultrasound recommendations. In the attributed narration, the speaker contrasts lung ultrasound, which interprets artifacts produced by the lung, with exams that directly show anatomy and pathology, then explains that lung-ultrasound profiles can overlap across conditions and do not map one-to-one to diagnoses such as pneumonia. The recommendation cover page remains on screen throughout. In the attributed narration, the speaker says clinicians combine lung-ultrasound findings with the patient’s clinical presentation, use overlapping profiles to weigh possibilities such as pneumonia, atelectasis, contusion, or fibrosis, and frames bedside ultrasound as collecting information at the bedside to support decisions. The recommendations cover remains through the first three Locals. The final frame of [750,760) introduces an “Evaluation for Pneumothorax” title slide; [760,780) shows a list of four sonographic findings: absent lung sliding, lung point, absent B-lines, and absent lung pulse. The attributed narration transitions to pneumothorax evaluation. The first three Local windows show the black slide listing four pneumothorax findings. [810,820) shows that slide before a white decision flowchart at 819 seconds; [820,840) shows paired grayscale lung ultrasound images, after a flowchart frame at 821 seconds. The attributed narration discusses lung sliding, its limited specificity when absent alone, and use of other findings such as lung point in a decision process. The visuals alternate between a pneumothorax decision flowchart, grayscale lung-ultrasound images, the four-findings list, and paired ultrasound images. In the attributed narration, the speaker describes the lung point as an edge where movement is seen on one side and absent on the other, then begins discussing B-lines as reverberation artifacts between pleural layers. Paired grayscale lung-ultrasound images dominate the visuals; a pneumothorax decision flowchart briefly reappears before the final ultrasound image. In the attributed narration, the speaker explains how B-line artifacts relate to pleural opposition and says their presence can help rule against pneumothorax, then introduces lung pulse as the final finding. A single grayscale lung-ultrasound view remains on screen throughout this block. In the attributed narration, the speaker describes lung pulse as faint rhythmic movement transmitted from the beating heart, says it is absent with pneumothorax, and recaps the absent signs used in the pneumothorax decision tree. The minute shows an “Evaluation of Interstitial Syndrome” title with intermittent black frames, then a “Definition of B Lines” slide from 1069 seconds. The definition slide lists discrete laser-like projections from the pleural line, reaching the bottom without fading and moving with lung sliding. The attributed narration introduces A-versus-B profiles and begins defining B-lines. The “Definition of B Lines” slide appears intermittently with black frames through the first four Locals and at the start of [1120,1130). By 1129 seconds, a “What Is a Positive Region?” slide defines a positive region as three or more B-lines in a longitudinal plane between ribs. The attributed narration discusses normal versus pathological B-line findings. The positive-region slide defines three or more B-lines between ribs in a longitudinal plane and remains through 1175 seconds. By 1179 seconds the presentation changes to a “Pathologies Associated with B Lines” list, which continues through the end of the minute. The attributed narration describes mapping positive regions and notes B-lines can occur with multiple conditions. The same black slide listing conditions associated with B-lines remains visible throughout. In the attributed narration, the speaker discusses overlap between COVID pneumonia and other interstitial pneumonia patterns, describes B-lines as a potentially helpful but nonspecific finding, and begins mentioning pulmonary fibrosis. The B-lines-associated conditions list remains through most of the block, then transitions to a “Questions to Ask” slide listing clinical scenario, unilateral versus bilateral distribution, homogeneous versus patchy pattern, and location. In the attributed narration, the speaker notes B-lines can occur across many conditions and emphasizes interpreting them in the patient’s clinical context, contrasting cough and fever with trauma. The “Questions to Ask” slide remains on screen throughout, listing clinical scenario, laterality, homogeneous versus patchy distribution, and location. In the attributed narration, the speaker explains that these questions help distinguish among possible causes of B-lines, contrasting diffuse bilateral patterns with focal or patchy findings and discussing anterior/posterior and apical/basal location. A static teaching graphic shows a torso marked with lung-zone divisions alongside annotated anterior and posterior body diagrams with numbered zones. The first Local briefly begins on the preceding “Questions to Ask” slide. In the attributed narration, the speaker introduces lung-zone mapping, describes anterior/lateral and posterior zones, and transitions toward clinical scenarios for interpreting B-profiles. A “Pulmonary Edema” slide remains throughout, pairing a grayscale lung-ultrasound image with labels for bilateral, homogeneous, smooth pleura, anterior, and apical. In the attributed narration, the speaker describes B-lines as a positive region and characterizes pulmonary edema as typically bilateral and relatively homogeneous, with possible gradation from apical to basal areas. The block begins with the pulmonary-edema ultrasound graphic, labeled bilateral, homogeneous, smooth pleura, anterior, and apical. In the final Local windows it transitions to an interstitial-pneumonia graphic labeled bilateral, patchy, subpleural consolidations, posterior, and basal. In the attributed narration, the speaker links edema patterns to gravity and smooth pleura, then contrasts that clinical context with cough and fever associated with possible COVID-era pneumonia. The “Interstitial Pneumonia” slide remains throughout, pairing a grayscale lung-ultrasound image with labels for bilateral, patchy, subpleural consolidations, posterior, and basal. In the attributed narration, the speaker contrasts this patchier pattern with pulmonary edema, describes posterior/basal distribution, and notes subpleural consolidations and an irregular rather than smooth pleural line. The first two Local windows continue the interstitial-pneumonia slide. The visuals then change to a “Pulmonary Fibrosis” slide labeled bilateral, fragmented pleura, and patchy; the final frame introduces an “ARDS” slide. In the attributed narration, the speaker describes a small subpleural consolidation, then contrasts a chronic pulmonary-fibrosis history with other clinical scenarios and begins discussing ARDS. The visuals begin on an ARDS slide labeled bilateral, patchy, fragmented pleura, and subpleural consolidations; they then change to an atelectasis slide labeled focal, posterior, basal, and smooth pleura, followed by a pulmonary-contusion slide. In the attributed narration, the speaker discusses ARDS monitoring, then describes atelectasis as often focal and posterior/inferior before beginning a contrast with pulmonary contusion. The pulmonary-contusion ultrasound slide, labeled unilateral, focal, and smooth pleura, remains for the first five Local windows. The final Local shows a black title slide reading “Evaluation for Lung Consolidation?” In the attributed narration, the speaker emphasizes that B-lines do not uniquely mean pulmonary edema and should be interpreted with other ultrasound and clinical clues, then introduces evaluation for lung consolidation. The visuals move from the lung-consolidation section title to a definition slide showing a grayscale ultrasound image and the criteria “subpleural, echo-poor space” and “tissue-like echo texture,” then to a list of associated pathologies: pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, lung cancer/metastases, atelectasis, and pulmonary contusion. In the attributed narration, the speaker defines consolidation, describes tissue-like echo texture, lists possible causes, and says clinical context guides interpretation.

global_summary_target: So far the lesson explains probe selection for pulmonary-edema assessment and introduces A-line/B-line artifact recognition. Schematics contrast horizontal reverberations with vertical artifacts beneath a line between ribs. local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The opening animation includes a title identifying the lesson as ultrasound of pulmonary edema, presented by Jacob Avila, MD. Narration introduces using ultrasound to identify pulmonary edema and begins discussing equipment. No diagnostic lung image is visible in the sampled opening.

Close views compare a linear transducer, a broad curvilinear transducer marked C6-2 and a smaller sector-shaped probe marked S4-2. Narration prefers the curvilinear probe while describing another option whose name is garbled as 'phase rail' in ASR. This window concerns equipment selection rather than lung findings.

A slide headed pulmonary edema lists artifact patterns A-lines and B-lines. Narration introduces artifact patterns used when assessing possible pulmonary edema. This is a teaching framework, without an individual patient's lung image or diagnosis in the sampled window.

The A-line and B-line artifact-pattern slide remains. Narration names both artifacts and emphasizes recognizing and using them clinically without detailing theories of their formation. This window is conceptual teaching, not a visual demonstration of either artifact in a patient.

A schematic depicts two gray rib profiles, a superficial connecting line and repeated horizontal white lines at increasing depth. Narration identifies ribs, the pleural-line region and A-lines as horizontal reverberation artifacts. The ASR says 'plural line'; the diagram is instructional and does not depict a patient-specific abnormality.

The schematic changes from repeated horizontal A-lines to long vertical B-lines arising below the superficial line between ribs. Narration associates A-lines with underlying air and uses them as a non-edema teaching mnemonic, then introduces B-lines. This contrast is the instructor's simplified explanation, not an exclusion of disease in a patient.

block_summary_target: The instructor defines B-lines as vertical artifacts extending from the pleural-line region to the image bottom and moving with respiration, with a garbled chest-radiograph comparison. Grayscale examples contrast horizontal A-line echoes and deep vertical bands, including paired cases interpreted by the speaker as non-edema and edema. The minute ends with an explicit caution that B-lines alone do not establish diagnosis; motion is not independently assessed from stills.
global_summary_target: The lesson has introduced curvilinear probe selection, schematic A-line/B-line patterns and grayscale examples contrasting horizontal reverberations with deep vertical bands. Narration links these patterns to pulmonary-edema assessment while emphasizing that B-lines alone are insufficient for diagnosis. Artifact motion and case interpretations remain attributed to the speaker rather than inferred from the sampled images.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The schematic shows several vertical lines extending from the superficial line between two rib profiles to the image bottom. The vertical-line schematic transitions to a grayscale lung example with a bright superficial horizontal interface and deeper horizontal echoes. Narration adds movement with respiration to the artifact definition and introduces an example said to lack pulmonary edema. Its chest-radiograph comparison contains garbled medical terms and is not expanded. Respiratory motion is not established from the still.

The grayscale lung example shows a bright superficial interface with repeated horizontal echoes and lateral shadowed regions. Narration identifies ribs and rib shadows, then calls the deeper horizontal artifact an A-line and repeats the air/non-edema mnemonic. A garbled landmark word is retained for listening review; the teaching interpretation is attributed to the instructor.

A new grayscale lung example shows multiple bright vertical bands arising from a bright superficial interface and extending deeply through the image. Narration identifies them as B-lines and begins explaining their implication. The visual pattern is described directly, while the unfinished diagnostic phrase is not completed from the next window.

Two lung ultrasound examples appear side by side: the left shows repeated horizontal echoes, while the right shows bright deep vertical bands. Narration contrasts the left as a non-edema example and the right as an edema example, with the disease word imperfectly transcribed. These are instructor-interpreted teaching cases, not a diagnosis from static pattern alone.

The paired horizontal- and vertical-artifact examples transition to a slide questioning the link between B-lines and pulmonary edema. Narration identifies vertical artifacts as B-lines but cautions that their presence or absence alone does not necessarily establish a diagnosis. This qualifies the earlier simplified pattern comparison.

block_summary_target: A four-zone hemithorax photograph with axillary-line markers and a chest diagram illustrate scanning distribution. Narration states that B-line pattern and location matter, discusses uncertainty in the commonly used dividing-line illustration and cites a third-intercostal-space convention. The instructor emphasizes an anterior/lateral four-zone survey and begins a two-zones-per-hemithorax criterion. These are protocol explanations rather than a patient's scan results.
global_summary_target: The lesson introduces probe choice, A-line/B-line schematics and lung examples, then cautions that artifacts alone do not establish pulmonary edema. It develops a distributed chest-zone survey using a four-zone hemithorax photograph and diagram, discusses dividing-line conventions and begins a bilateral-zone criterion. All diagnostic implications and dynamic artifact definitions remain attributed to instruction rather than inferred from static images.

local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The B-line diagnostic-question slide transitions to a photograph of a hemithorax divided by black lines into four numbered zones with AAL and PAL markers. The four-zone thorax photograph remains, with anterior and posterior axillary-line abbreviations and numbered regions. The same four-zone hemithorax illustration remains on screen. Narration describes dividing each hemithorax into four equal zones and comments that this commonly used photograph is confusing. The beginning of the dividing-line phrase is corrupted in ASR, so no specific extra landmark is supplied.

The four-zone photograph transitions to an anterior thorax/lung diagram with a thick horizontal divider. Narration says the cited article places the transverse line at the third intercostal space, higher than the photograph suggests, and begins describing the instructor's practical division. This is a discussion of zone convention, not a patient anatomical abnormality.

The anterior chest/lung diagram with a horizontal divider remains. Narration describes dividing the survey into four equal zones and contrasts the importance of posterior scanning for other pulmonary pathology with its role in this edema-focused approach. The speaker's protocol emphasis is not taken as evidence of absent posterior disease.

The chest-zone diagram remains as narration instructs placing the probe in the defined zones and looking for A-lines or B-lines. The instructor introduces a pattern of B-lines in two zones per hemithorax, but the concluding interpretation is unfinished in this window. No actual chest contact or lung scan is shown here.

block_summary_target: Schematics and a brief anterior chest probe demonstration accompany the B-line counting discussion. The recap defines a positive zone as at least three B-lines and the stated diffuse-edema pattern as at least two positive zones per side. local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The chest-zone diagram transitions to schematics with first one and then two long vertical lines beneath the superficial interface between ribs. The recap slide pairs three or more B-lines for a positive zone with two or more zones per side under the pulmonary-edema heading. The threshold recap slide transitions to another grayscale lung example containing deep vertical bright bands. local_sub_summaries.local_summary_target: The tutorial introduces transthoracic lung ultrasound and compares probe choices.
A linear probe resolves the pleural line well but attenuates more and shows deeper structures less clearly.

For a broader lung examination, the presenters favor a phased-array probe.
The phased-array probe provides adequate pleural-line views and better visualization of deeper structures.
Its small footprint also reduces rib-shadowing limitations at lateral and posterior chest sites.
